title: The Rise of the Legal Quants (Jamie Tso & Raymond Sun)
author: Jamie Tso · Raymond Sun

dom.t: Legal products: Expertise and design outrank model access

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source provides only promotional and organisational information about Legal Quants’ member showcase, discussion digest and social channels. It offers no substantive claim or evidence about pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, transformation, or forecast autonomous workflows, so its position relative to the cluster proposition cannot be determined.
qs: That's where we showcase all members' profiles and their projects.
We also run a sub stack, so that's where we post key discussions, weekly digest of the discussions that we have as a group.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core expectation that AI will reshape legal delivery beyond isolated task automation and materially extends it with a specific prospective model: specialised practices exposed through agent-accessible APIs and client-facing platforms. It also identifies fragmented interfaces, high switching costs and the absence of a neutral marketplace as barriers, while offering qualitative forecasts rather than evidence of market-wide transformation.
qs: But as we see that legal services become more liquid, then there is a market for these services, and we see that more and more law firms and their practices may turn their practices into an API on an endpoint, where AI agents can simply call, and that becomes a really liquid legal marketplace.
So the legal market is the interface that is fragmented that way, because there's no neutral marketplace for that.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s implementation-focused premise and materially extends it with a concrete service-redesign example: using AI to replace a simple transaction-value threshold with multifactor risk assessment. It also identifies deep domain expertise and system design as prerequisites, while offering no measured evidence of reliability or operational outcomes.
qs: Instead, we should use AI to take a look at the variety of different factors to assess the risk of that transaction.

So this also requires a lot of domain expertise because knowing what actually affects the risk of that transaction requires deep domain expertise, requires a lot of experience in proven transactions, and how the traditional dollar threshold model breaks.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI shifts value away from labour-intensive production and billable-hour economics while preserving a premium for AI-fluent legal expertise. It materially extends the cluster with a speculative marketplace model in which firms expose services through APIs and clients or agents access lawyer-created tools directly, although this goes beyond the cluster’s stronger evidence for bounded, human-reviewed automation.
qs: I think that the people shift is the bigger play here, because we see that a lot of the economic value will be shifted from people that are not as fluent to people that are very fluent in AI.
But definitely as these friction points get increasingly like removed, that's where the pricing crunch kind of gets squeezed.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends chiefly on human capability, adoption and organisational change rather than tool availability alone. It materially extends the cluster by predicting a specific redesign of legal delivery: specialised practices packaged as agent-callable services and client-facing tools, while acknowledging scarce implementation talent and unresolved market fragmentation. Its marketplace claims are predictions, not evidence of realised outcomes.
qs: And the how, that how question, 80% or even 90% is a human problem.

But as we see that legal services become more liquid, then there is a market for these services, and we see that more and more law firms and their practices may turn their practices into an API on an endpoint, where AI agents can simply call, and that becomes a really liquid legal marketplace.

st.t: Legal products: Expertise and design outrank model access
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that competitive advantage comes from combining legal expertise with the ability to design, configure and deploy AI systems, rather than merely obtaining a leading tool. Its workflow examples and human-capability emphasis reinforce that framing, while its performance and commercial claims remain conditional or prospective rather than independently demonstrated.
qs: They say they believe the next generation of elite legal work won't be defined by those who have the best AI tool, but by who has the rare ability to design, evaluate, and deploy any tool available to them to reimagine how legal services are created and consumed.

So this also requires a lot of domain expertise because knowing what actually affects the risk of that transaction requires deep domain expertise, requires a lot of experience in proven transactions, and how the traditional dollar threshold model breaks.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on practitioner–engineer collaboration and legal workflow-specific tooling through firsthand accounts of regulatory mapping, document automation and an iteratively developed AI-regulation tracker. Its support is limited: it does not substantively address human verification, professional accountability or whether specialist workflow layers can defend durable value against improving general models.
qs: So what I did back then was I reached out to some machine learning engineers on Upwork, and then I worked together to build some small language models using TensorFlow, and do entity mapping.
Along the way, each thing that I learned, whether it be from generative AI all the way to agents, each project of Aboctol is kind of like a feature to that tracker.

kp.k: LegalQuants prioritise redesign over incremental workflow optimisation
kp.d: Tso defines LegalQuants as lawyers who combine domain expertise and system design to rethink how legal services are created and consumed from the client's perspective. His distinction from legal engineers is the group's own conceptual framing: engineers optimise existing workflows, while LegalQuants seek new opportunities and markets using AI, drawing on a financial-market analogy of finding alpha.
qs: So a legal engineer is someone that looks at existing workflow and think, how do I optimize it?
A LegalQuant look at existing workflow and think, how do I redesign the whole thing from first principles?
They look for new opportunities, they look for new markets.

kp.k: Lawyer-built tools address otherwise underserved operational tasks
kp.d: The guests offer first-person implementation accounts rather than systematic evidence. Tso reports that experimentation with an AI Prompt connector in late 2024 led to a tool used by 18 offices worldwide, supported by daily colleague feedback. Sun describes building extraction and formatting tools for needs too small for vendors to address, alongside ordinary legal work.
qs: I think it was late 2024 when they introduced this connector called AI Prompt
I built a tool that went viral and that got used to by 18 offices worldwide.
all of the stuff that annoying for lawyers, but not big enough for legal tech vendors to really actually solve for you.
I was basically building these tools while I was doing my day-to-day law jobs.

kp.k: AI-assisted coding expands lawyers' ability to build products
kp.d: Tso describes moving from no-code Power Automate to AI-assisted coding as platforms became more capable. He reports experimenting with reproducing features of established legal tools and open-sourcing a review tool. The account illustrates perceived reductions in development barriers, but also acknowledges that an early replication attempt exposed a substantial functionality gap.
qs: I thought I need to build better products, I need to use better tools, so I started experimenting with Replit.
But then quickly we see that these VypCoding platforms have been more and more capable.
So I started off replicating the spellbook to see where the gap is.
It was obviously much bigger back then because it involves Stalks manipulation and so on.

kp.k: Practitioner examples illustrate new AI-enabled service designs
kp.d: Tso reports two examples without providing outcome measurements: a US special counsel's system monitors stock-price declines, dispatches agents to seek evidence of fraud and drafts potential claims; a UAE counsel's board-authority tool assesses multiple transaction-risk factors rather than allocating approval solely by monetary thresholds. He presents both as requiring substantial legal domain knowledge, not merely faster execution of existing processes.
qs: There is a special council in the US who created this solution where it looks at the stock prices every day, see who drops the most, and automatically dispatch AI agents to look for evidence of secret fraud, automatically draft statement of claim for potential plaintiff.
Instead, we should use AI to take a look at the variety of different factors to assess the risk of that transaction.
So this also requires a lot of domain expertise because knowing what actually affects the risk of that transaction requires deep domain expertise

kp.k: Human capabilities matter more than ownership of particular tools
kp.d: Sun argues that rapidly changing tools make technical understanding, first-principles reasoning, creativity and practical deployment the durable sources of advantage. His statements that software costs are approaching zero and that implementation is 80% or 90% a human problem are speaker assertions, not reported study findings. He emphasises upskilling, adoption, culture and education as determinants of impact.
qs: the cost of software is basically going to zero
It's only those who really understand how the tool works, and also can really think on first principles and apply it to actual real-world cases and deliver real impact, right?
And the how, that how question, 80% or even 90% is a human problem.
And this is where all the up-skilling, human adoption, culture, education, all that stuff gets wrapped in there.

kp.d: Tso reports that an open LinkedIn group attracted a few hundred members overnight but generated no posting, whereas an invitation-only WhatsApp group produced substantial engagement. He attributes the difference partly to a nonjudgmental environment and describes hackathons, project sharing and mapping community discussions as ways to support collaboration. Member feedback about previously building alone is anecdotal evidence of an unmet professional-community need.
qs: overnight there are a few hundred people who joined. But then the group is dead.
Part of that is because we have made that into a safe space, where people can talk about things without fearing judgment.
before this group, everyone felt like they're the only one building things, they're building in silo.
they feel like they found their people, they found their tribe

kp.k: Specialist legal services could become agent-accessible marketplaces
kp.d: Tso predicts that faster delivery will make specialised legal services more liquid, with firms exposing practices through APIs that AI agents can call and clients using lawyer-created tools directly. He cites client-facing platforms as a directional sign, but leaves unresolved whether a central marketplace or multiple marketplaces will emerge, and whether model companies or legal-tech companies would control them. Existing panels, switching costs and fragmented interfaces are barriers in his account.
qs: more and more law firms and their practices may turn their practices into an API on an endpoint, where AI agents can simply call
clients will be able to use legal services directly, without actually engaging with their lawyers
will there be one centralized marketplace?
Or whether there will be a lot of different marketplaces?
the switching cost between law firms for clients and their clients are pretty high

kp.k: AI fluency may redistribute professional economic value
kp.d: Tso anticipates economic value shifting towards highly AI-fluent lawyers, while the specific outputs they produce evolve from applications to skills and autonomous agents. He describes LegalQuants' role as finding, connecting and deploying such talent, initially potentially through recruitment but eventually through other markets. Sun similarly argues that unusually impactful talent needs recognition, career control and compensation commensurate with its contribution; these are aspirations and forecasts, not measured labour-market outcomes.
qs: a lot of the economic value will be shifted from people that are not as fluent to people that are very fluent in AI.
Today, it could be if I put in some apps, tomorrow is creating skills, the day after it could be creating autonomous agents.
really getting 10x the benefits for being for being 10x impactful.

kp.k: Speed and scarce capability could justify output-based pricing
kp.d: Tso supports pricing output rather than time and argues that, where advice is equivalent, delivering it in five minutes rather than five hours should command more because speed differentiates the service. He also predicts that lawyers who monitor new regulations and respond at software speed could capture or monopolise emerging advisory areas. These are conditional pricing and competitive-positioning arguments, not evidence of achieved premiums.
qs: Everyone's talking about measuring value based on the output rather than the time you put in. I think there is some merits to it.
to the extent the advice is the same and it's commoditized, then the speed becomes a differentiator
that piece of advice should cost more than if you were to just turn out the same advice in five hours.
The lawyer that is able to monitor these signals, quickly give advice in relation to those new regulations, deliver the same at the speed of software, has a chance of monopolizing that new area.

kp.k: Automation shifts pricing towards risk transfer and revenue creation
kp.d: Sun frames traditional legal fees as payment for friction or risk transfer, with hourly billing pricing intellectual and manual effort. He predicts that AI's removal of friction will squeeze those fees and push firms and vendors towards charging for assumed risk or new client revenue opportunities. He argues that a pure cost-saving proposition increasingly struggles to sustain good margins; the dollar examples are illustrative, not observed returns.
qs: pricing is basically just a reflection of either your pricing for friction or your pricing for risk transfer.
as these friction points get increasingly like removed, that's where the pricing crunch kind of gets squeezed.
So you pay us more, but we take on risk for you.
For every $1 you pay us, we can help you make $5 back in your own business.
The whole saving cost narrative has suddenly become increasingly hard to make good margins.

kp.k: Alternative IP arrangements could incentivise internal innovation
kp.d: Asked by Main about billable-hour resistance to efficiency tools, Sun instead centres the intrapreneur's dilemma on ownership of employee-created intellectual property and incentives. He describes firm ownership as the current model, without presenting a legal analysis, and recommends exploring compensation, other benefits, shared ownership or licensing. He suggests that a firm's willingness to try such arrangements could attract builder talent.
qs: I think the intrapreneur's dilemma is, at its very principle, is the question around IP.
Obviously, the traditional current model is employees' IP is firms' IP.
Could we look at 50-50? Could we look at licensing options?
to really try these new IP arrangements, that could be the secret unlock to attracting the talent that you need.

kp.k: Configured general-purpose AI may outperform packaged tools conditionally
kp.d: Responding to Main's question about the group's Claude testing, Tso argues that developer-friendly tools offer skilled operators control over configuration, debugging and workflow design. He says comparing unconfigured Claude with purpose-built legal software is unfair and predicts that a skilled lawyer using a tailored system can outperform an average lawyer using an average legal-tech tool. He warns that out-of-the-box use can be dangerous. The response gives no test protocol, sample or quantified comparative results; the 1% utilisation statement is explicitly his impression.
qs: I think that only 1% of us actually utilize the full potential of Claude code itself
What makes Claude for Word useful for legal is if you design the skills that help you do your legal work
how do you design your own workflow, how do you debug if things are not working, how can you make it better, how can you tweak your skill.
it's dangerous if you just use it out of the box.
With that combination, creates a scenario where it can actually outperform, just an average lawyer using an average legal tech tool.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jamie Tso argues that AI enables lawyers to redesign legal services from first principles rather than merely accelerate existing workflows.
pts.d: Tso distinguishes the LegalQuant approach from his characterization of legal engineering as incremental workflow optimization. His examples are an agent-based system for identifying potential litigation and drafting claims, and a board delegation tool that evaluates transaction risk using multiple factors rather than monetary thresholds alone. He presents these as new ways to practice law requiring legal domain expertise and system-design skills.

pts.k: Ray Sun predicts that human talent and implementation capability, rather than possession of a particular tool, will determine who realizes AI's benefits.
pts.d: Sun argues that falling software-development costs and rapidly changing products make creativity, first-principles thinking, adoption, education and culture more durable sources of advantage. He describes 80–90% of the challenge of delivering real impact as a human problem; the percentages are his characterization, not a reported measurement. Tso similarly predicts economic value will shift toward lawyers who are highly fluent in AI.

pts.k: Tso predicts a more liquid legal-services market in which firms expose services through APIs and clients access lawyer-created tools directly.
pts.d: Tso anticipates AI agents calling law-firm service endpoints, and lawyers creating replicas or tools that clients can use without directly engaging them for each interaction. He points to AI-native firms' client-facing platforms and legal-AI vendors' portals as directional signs. He leaves unresolved whether transactions will converge on one centralized marketplace or multiple marketplaces, and whether a model company or legal-tech company might own such a market. He identifies existing client switching costs and fragmented firm interfaces as obstacles.

pts.k: Tso argues that rapid AI-enabled advice can justify premium output-based pricing and create opportunities to dominate newly emerging regulatory niches.
pts.d: Tso's pricing argument is conditional on equivalent advice quality and on advice being sufficiently standardized or commoditized. He argues that delivering the same advice in minutes rather than hours should command a higher price. He also predicts that lawyers who detect regulatory changes and deliver otherwise unavailable advice at software speed could gain pricing power or potentially monopolize a new area. These are proposed market mechanisms, not reported pricing outcomes.

pts.k: Sun predicts that AI's removal of work-related friction will squeeze traditional legal pricing and push providers toward charging for risk transfer or client revenue creation.
pts.d: Sun characterizes much current legal pricing, including hourly billing, as payment for the intellectual and manual friction involved in producing work. As AI removes those chargeable activities, he expects margin pressure and a shift toward other value propositions: assuming clients' risk or helping them generate revenue. His dollar-return examples are illustrative, not empirical results.

pts.k: Sun suggests that alternative intellectual-property and compensation arrangements could help firms attract and reward lawyer-builders.
pts.d: Sun frames the intrapreneur's dilemma primarily as an incentive and IP-control problem. Alongside compensation and other benefits, he proposes exploring shared ownership or licensing rather than treating ownership as an all-or-nothing choice. He presents improved talent attraction as a possible benefit of experimentation, not an established result.

pts.k: Tso claims that skilled lawyers configuring general-purpose, developer-friendly AI can outperform average lawyers using ordinary legal-tech products.
pts.d: Discussing Claude tools, Tso emphasizes the operator's ability to create skills, customize workflows and debug behavior. He argues that an out-of-the-box comparison between a general-purpose platform and a dedicated legal product misses this configuration advantage. His claim concerns a skilled operator–tool combination, not autonomous superiority of an unconfigured model or the inevitable displacement of legal-AI vendors. He also warns that using such tools without learning how to operate them can be dangerous.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The speakers support their claims primarily with personal building experience, community examples and conceptual reasoning rather than quantitative studies.
pts.d: Tso reports progressing from unsuccessful early machine-learning experiments to an internal Power Automate tool used in 18 offices, then experimenting with AI-assisted coding and replicating legal-tech features. Sun reports building document-automation infrastructure, small tools for unmet lawyer needs and an AI-regulation tracker. These experiences support their claims about lawyer-led development, but the transcript supplies no measured productivity, accuracy, revenue or client-outcome results. Tso's litigation and delegation examples concern unnamed practitioners, with no detailed performance evidence. The marketplace, pricing and IP-incentive claims are extrapolations and proposals. Although asked about stress-testing Claude, Tso provides no test protocol, sample, scores or controlled comparison; his account instead explains the importance of operator skill and configuration.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview combines reported present capabilities with undated future predictions; its strongest claims depend on expertise, configuration, standardization and institutional change.
pts.d: In the source labeled 2026, Tso dates his more serious internal AI-workflow experimentation to late 2024 and describes the LegalQuants community as a concentrated force for roughly three months. The speakers present lawyer-built tools and workflow redesign as already occurring. Liquid marketplaces, redistribution of economic value and new pricing models are future directions without deadlines; references to today, tomorrow and the day after describe a progression rather than a dated forecast. Premium pricing depends on equivalent advice and speed-based differentiation, while market dominance requires timely advice others cannot supply. General-purpose AI performance depends on skilled configuration. IP-based talent attraction depends on firms being willing to experiment. Tso explicitly leaves marketplace concentration and ownership unresolved.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect lawyer-builders, less AI-fluent lawyers, law firms, corporate clients and legal-AI vendors in different ways.
pts.d: AI-fluent lawyer-builders are the proposed beneficiaries of greater economic value, new markets and potentially better IP-based rewards; less fluent lawyers may lose relative economic advantage. Traditional and AI-native law firms face workflow redesign, changing service interfaces, pressure on friction-based billing and a need to retain technical legal talent. Clients may consume legal services directly through platforms and agents, buy faster advice, or pay for risk transfer and revenue creation. Specialized regulatory practices are highlighted as candidates for software-speed delivery. Boards and managers feature in Tso's risk-based delegation example, and potential plaintiffs in his litigation-agent example. Legal-AI vendors face comparison with lawyer-configured general-purpose tools and possible competition over marketplace ownership. The source does not make a specific access-to-justice prediction for underserved individuals.
